name: Fungal acne protocol (Malassezia)

lead: Fungal acne is the popular name for Malassezia (pityrosporum) folliculitis, where yeast that normally lives on skin overgrows in hair follicles and causes itchy, uniform bumps, most often on the upper trunk and sometimes the forehead. The online protocol aims to clear those bumps for smoother forehead and body skin by avoiding certain oils and using antifungal treatments.

Malassezia are lipophilic yeasts that need fatty acids to grow, which is the basis for the avoid-certain-oils idea. The condition is recognised in dermatology and treated with antifungals. On looksmax.org, users report forehead bumps and flaking and say ordinary acne approaches did not help. The product-avoidance rules circulating online have not been tested as a whole.

paras: People check ingredient lists for fatty-acid-containing oils and use antifungal washes or treatments, often alongside dandruff or seborrheic dermatitis care. Diagnosis is clinical and based on distribution, and persistent bumps are generally assessed by a dermatologist.

Malassezia are part of normal skin flora and are linked to several skin conditions, including seborrheic dermatitis, so self-diagnosis from forums can be mistaken. Antifungal treatments are generally chosen with a dermatologist or pharmacist when bumps persist.

angle.text: Itchy, uniform bumps on the forehead or body are sometimes yeast-driven, and people cut fatty-acid oils and use antifungal washes to reduce the overgrowth and smooth the skin. Malassezia folliculitis is a recognised condition treated with antifungals, though self-diagnosis in forums is common.

lead: Fungal acne is a popular name for Malassezia folliculitis, also called pityrosporum folliculitis: a skin condition in which yeast of the genus Malassezia, a normal part of human skin flora, overgrows within hair follicles and produces itchy, uniform papules and pustules.[1][2][3] Despite the name it is not acne vulgaris. Dermatology sources separate the two mainly by the absence of comedones (blackheads and whiteheads) and by the prominent itch.[3]

For people trying to improve their skin, the term matters because bumps on the forehead, hairline, chest and back that do not respond to usual acne routines are sometimes attributed to this yeast, and because the usual first-line acne products work through different mechanisms. In looksmaxxing and skincare forums, 'fungal acne' also names a protocol: avoiding oils and ingredients that contain the fatty acids Malassezia feeds on, choosing products described as 'fungal-acne safe', and using antifungal washes or creams. Looksmax.org threads show users describing forehead bumps and flaking, sometimes alongside seborrheic dermatitis, and asking what to use.[4][5]

Wikipedia describes the condition as occurring most often on the upper trunk (back, chest, arms) in young to middle-aged adults, with overgrowth associated with oily skin, humidity and conditions such as seborrheic dermatitis or severe dandruff.[1] Malassezia are lipophilic, depending on fatty acids found in skin oils to multiply.[1][2] The condition, its causative yeasts and its treatment with antifungals are described in the dermatology literature; the online protocol as a whole, including its ingredient-avoidance rules, has not been trialled.

paras: Malassezia folliculitis arises when Malassezia furfur and related species overgrow and plug hair follicles, producing itchy papules and pustules in a follicular pattern. Diagnosis rests on the pattern and location of lesions.[1] DermNet describes it as an infection of the hair follicle and oil gland by lipophilic yeasts, mainly M. globosa, M. sympodialis and M. restricta, that normally live on the skin and cause disease only under certain conditions.[3]

The genus now includes about 14 species of yeast found on all skin surfaces of humans and animals as commensals that can also act as pathogens; molecular studies found Malassezia DNA predominantly on the core body and arms, where sebaceous glands are dense.[6] Pityriasis versicolor is the only skin disease etiologically tied to Malassezia, while in folliculitis, seborrheic dermatitis and others the yeasts are suggested to contribute.[2]

The eruption is monomorphic: the lesions all look alike, a few millimetres across, and itchy. DermNet lists the upper back and chest as the main sites, with the forehead and hairline, chin, neck and outer upper arms also affected, and notes that the absence of comedones is the key distinction from acne vulgaris.[3] It can resemble steroid acne and bacterial folliculitis, and DermNet says diagnosis is often delayed.[3] Grokipedia adds that the lesions typically lack cysts and do not usually scar.[7]

Wikipedia lists oily skin, humidity and pre-existing conditions such as seborrheic dermatitis and severe dandruff.[1] DermNet adds hot, humid climates, excessive sweating, occlusion from emollients and sunscreens, antibiotic use and immunosuppression including topical or oral steroids.[3] A T Nation poster in 2007 likewise suggested that the condition can follow sweat, tight clothing and follicular damage and is common among athletes.[8]

Wikipedia credits the French physician Louis-Charles Malassez with identifying the genus in the late 1800s and linking it to seborrheic dermatitis; Baillon named the genus Malassezia in 1889, and in 1904 Raymond Sabouraud described a dandruff-associated organism as Pityrosporum malassezii. Because both names referred to the same yeast, Malassezia took priority, which is why the folliculitis is still called pityrosporum folliculitis in older literature and forums.[9][1] The genus is the only one in its family, order and class (Malasseziomycetes, defined in 2014), and naming was complicated because the yeasts need special media and grow slowly.[9] Index Fungorum lists 22 species, with M. globosa responsible for most human skin disease and M. restricta also involved.[9]

Most Malassezia species cannot make their own long-chain fatty acids and must take them from the skin or from products on it. Wikipedia reports that Malassezia grows by consuming fatty acids with chain lengths of about 11 to 24 carbons.[1] The Malassezia article describes this lipid dependence as the reason the yeasts cluster on oily, sebaceous areas such as the scalp, face and upper back, and notes that M. globosa produces several lipases and phospholipases to break down skin oils.[9]

This lipid dependence is the rationale behind the online ingredient-avoidance protocol: if the yeast feeds on certain fatty acids, products that contain them or their derivatives could in principle provide more fuel. Proponents say checking ingredient lists and selecting products marketed as fungal-acne safe has helped their bumps; Grokipedia's account of prevention likewise lists gentle cleansers and lightweight, oil-free moisturizers alongside reducing occlusion.[7] DermNet lists occlusion from emollients and sunscreens as a risk factor but gives no ingredient list or diet advice.[3] Product-avoidance regimens as a whole have not been tested in trials.

sections.h: How it differs from acne vulgaris
paras: Acne vulgaris involves comedones and a mix of lesion types, while Malassezia folliculitis is uniform and lacks comedones, according to DermNet.[3] Research comparing seborrheic dermatitis and Malassezia folliculitis has characterised the inflammatory cells and mediators in both.[10] A registered clinical study, started in 2018, compared Malassezia species proportions in inflammatory and non-inflammatory facial acne lesions in 120 people with acne vulgaris, reflecting ongoing interest in the yeast's role in ordinary acne.[11] A 2009 study concluded that the folliculitis is caused by cutaneous resident Malassezia species rather than an outside organism.[12]

sections.h: Treatment as described by dermatology sources
paras: DermNet says predisposing factors should be addressed first, then lists topical options such as selenium sulfide shampoo, ketoconazole or econazole, which work for most people but may need longer courses, with weekly use sometimes helping prevent recurrence; oral antifungals may work better than topical ones, with fluconazole preferred over itraconazole for its side-effect profile, though trial results are inconsistent.[3] Isotretinoin and photodynamic therapy have had some success in small case series of resistant disease.[3] A 2010 report described photodynamic therapy for recalcitrant Malassezia folliculitis.[13] Evidence-based Danish guidelines address treatment of Malassezia-related skin diseases generally.[14]

Recurrence is common even after successful treatment, and DermNet says long-term topical prophylaxis may be considered for people with repeated recurrences.[3] Reviews of seborrheic dermatitis, the related condition, describe antifungal and anti-inflammatory topicals as the most commonly used treatment, with ketoconazole as the mainstay for the face and body.[15][16]

Seborrheic dermatitis is a chronic, recurring condition of flaking, redness and itch in oil-rich areas, usually described as an inflammatory response to Malassezia, with three generally agreed contributors: sebaceous lipid secretion, Malassezia colonisation and immune dysregulation.[15][16][17] Many forum posts pair it with fungal acne.[4] A 2024 systematic review examined diet, obesity, supplements and alcohol in seborrheic dermatitis because each of those might modulate the lipid, yeast and inflammation pathways.[18] A 2022 review of atopic dermatitis names Malassezia among microbes proposed to contribute there.[19] Reviews also note that Malassezia infections can be a medical conundrum and can cause more serious disease in immunocompromised patients.[20][21]

Forum discussion of the topic is older than the current 'fungal acne' label. A 2007 T Nation thread told a poster that bumps on the back might be pityrosporum folliculitis rather than ordinary back acne, that antibacterial acne products would not help because the cause is fungal, and that it is common in athletes.[8] A 2009 thread has a poster saying that a daily anti-dandruff shampoo used as body wash cleared shoulder and back bumps within about two weeks after reading about the idea on another forum, and a 2024 poster reported that an antifungal cream nearly cleared bumps on the back and shoulders after a few uses.[22][23]

On looksmax.org the topic appears as forehead and temple bumps. One user reports both seborrheic dermatitis and fungal acne on the forehead and asks what to use; another says they have tried everything, including diet, and the problem is worsening.[4][5] Other members ask for photos before commenting, reflecting that the label is applied informally and without examination.[4] Mainstream sources describe diagnosis as clinical, confirmed where needed by microscopy of skin scrapings.[1][3]

Adherents of the protocol say that because the yeast feeds on certain fatty acids, products containing such oils can worsen bumps and that avoiding them, alongside antifungal products, helps. Forum users describe forehead bumps and flaking that they attribute to fungal acne and report that general skin-care and dietary changes did not resolve them.[4][5]

Wikipedia reports Malassezia growth depends on fatty acids of about 11 to 24 carbons.[1] Dermatology reviews describe the yeasts as normal flora that contribute to disease under conditions such as sebum excess, humidity or immune suppression.[2][20] The protocol's specific rules about which ingredients to avoid have not been compared against standard care in published trials, and DermNet recommends seeing a dermatologist for skin concerns.[3]

Human studies exist on Malassezia folliculitis and related disease, including immunohistochemical work on the skin lesions,[10] Danish treatment guidelines,[14] a photodynamic therapy report for resistant cases,[13] and a registered study of Malassezia proportions in acne vulgaris lesions.[11] Randomized and controlled trials of antifungal treatment exist mainly for seborrheic dermatitis.[15][16][17] No studies found testing the full online fungal acne protocol of avoiding fatty-acid ingredients.

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, fungal acne appears in threads where users with stubborn forehead bumps or flaking ask for product recommendations, often alongside seborrheic dermatitis; older T Nation threads discuss the same idea as pityrosporum folliculitis and back acne.[4][5][8]

timeline.event: Louis-Charles Malassez identifies the yeast genus and links it to seborrheic dermatitis.[9]
Raymond Sabouraud describes a dandruff-associated organism as Pityrosporum malassezii; the names later merge under Malassezia.[9]
A controlled trial tests 2% ketoconazole shampoo in androgenic alopecia, reflecting interest in scalp yeast.[24]
Immunohistochemistry study compares inflammatory cells in seborrheic dermatitis and Pityrosporum folliculitis.[10]
Study concludes Malassezia folliculitis is caused by cutaneous resident Malassezia species.[12]
Photodynamic therapy reported for recalcitrant Malassezia folliculitis.[13]
Malasseziomycetes is formally defined as a fungal class; JAAD publishes 'Malassezia infections: a medical conundrum'.[9][20]
Danish evidence-based treatment guidelines for Malassezia-related skin diseases; review reports 14 recognised species.[14][6]
A registered study begins comparing Malassezia species in inflammatory and non-inflammatory acne lesions in 120 people.[11]
